08f0f8c5dcd8: Chapter 11 describes the fellowship in "a certain western city" (p. 153), Akron (p. 156, later footnote), as it was when the book was written. Members met informally in each other's homes most evenings, and it became customary to "set apart one night a week for a meeting" (p. 159), open to anyone or everyone interested in a spiritual way of life. Its prime object was "to provide a time and place where new people might bring their problems" (p. 160).

"Many a distracted wife has visited this house to find loving and understanding companionship among women who knew her problem" (p. 160). Others held public or semipublic meetings with members speaking on the platform.
2bf366333161: Bill thought too much caution was a mistake. Groups that held no meetings except those for alcoholics only, year after year, would grow slowly: "Such groups are apt to grow slowly." (P-17, "Anonymity", 1946). In the usual course, "Little by little some meetings are opened to families and close friends." 07157bfa771d: Both co-founders got their start in the Oxford Group, a Christian movement of the 1930s. Bill W. came to it through his friend Ebby in late 1934; Dr. Bob had been going to its meetings in Akron for about two and a half years.

Bill said these came "straight from the Oxford Groups" and from its American leader, the Rev. Sam Shoemaker.
66a510757503: The alcoholics left because some Oxford Group ways did not work with drunks: pressure and aggressive evangelism, "team guidance," the "absolutes" as a dose too strong at first, and an emphasis on prominent names that clashed with the alcoholics' wish to stay anonymous. The Oxford Group also aimed to change the whole world, while the alcoholics kept to alcoholics.
c2deb9508cd6: New York separated in 1937. Cleveland's members broke away in May 1939, and Akron's late in 1939. The 1939 Big Book never names the Oxford Group.
de70a1bb3dd0: <0>The 1939 Big Book</0> describes the program but doesn't name the Oxford Group anywhere in its text. Bill's friend simply has "a simple religious idea and a practical program of action" (p. 9).
730c24baa491: <0>The 1955 Foreword to the Second Edition</0> gives the connection in one sentence: the broker had met "an alcoholic friend who had been in contact with the Oxford Groups of that day" (pp. xv–xvi). 1b7848bf989c: <0>Dr. Bob, 1948</0> (his last major talk, printed in P-53). Both men had been associated with the Oxford Group, "Bill in New York, for five months, and I in Akron, for two and a half years" (P-53). The one thing they hadn't told him was what Bill did that first Sunday: "attempt to be helpful to somebody else." (P-53). 5c4933f4af57: Why they separated (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957)

60d7cbb98a29: The book says what the stories are for: each writer tells "in his own language and from his own point of view" (p. 29) how he found his relationship with God, so a reader can recognize himself and say, "Yes, I am one of them too" (p. 29).

af4506bd36f5: How the Big Book describes its own parts
555c3c02e786: <0>Chapter 2, "There Is a Solution" (1939).</0> The book lays out its plan: chapters explaining alcoholism and addressing the agnostic, then "Further on, clear-cut directions are given showing how we recovered. Their purpose is identification: the authors believe that only by disclosing themselves will readers be "persuaded to say, 'Yes, I am one of them too; I must have this thing.'" (p. 29).
3a1dfa85480b: <0>Chapter 4, "We Agnostics" (1939).</0> The stories are where the book shows how differently members understand God: "In our personal stories you will find a wide variation in the way each teller approaches and conceives of the Power which is greater than himself." 27e39e19e8ab: <0>Chapter 5, "How It Works" (1939).</0> The chapter moves from the stories to the program: "Our stories disclose in a general way what we used to be like, what happened, and what we are like now." (p. 58). Then, for a reader who wants what they have: "Here are the steps we took, which are suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59).
d54ed5205d99: <0>The story section itself.</0> Its title page says the stories show "How Forty-Two Alcoholics Recovered From Their Malady" (p. 165), and each part has its own aim: Part I shows "that sobriety in A.A. can be lasting," Part II may help a reader decide whether he is alcoholic and whether A.A. is for him, and Part III offers hope to those who think their drinking hopeless (p. 167).

cb005b986ca0: What is "the phenomenon of craving," and what is the "allergy"? | Recovery Starts
8ad490e9037f: Both phrases come from Dr. William D. Silkworth's statement in "The Doctor's Opinion" at the front of the Big Book, kept as he wrote it in 1939 (p. xi).…
ce13eda8edaa: What is "the phenomenon of craving," and what is the "allergy"?
2559220d0075: Both phrases come from Dr. William D. Silkworth's statement in "The Doctor's Opinion" at the front of the Big Book, kept as he wrote it in 1939 (p. xi). He suggests that alcohol's action on chronic alcoholics is "a manifestation of an allergy" and that "the phenomenon of craving is limited to this class and never occurs in the average temperate drinker" (p. xxviii).
cc99ef79b0a1: In his account the craving is set off by drinking. These alcoholics "cannot start drinking without developing the phenomenon of craving" (p. xxx). The only relief he knows is "entire abstinence" (p. xxx).
d5b7d14ae13c: Quoted alone, "allergy" can sound like settled medicine. In its setting it's a theory: Silkworth says the craving "may be the manifestation of an allergy" (p. xxx), and the A.A. members who introduce him call it "The doctor's theory," saying that as laymen their opinion of it "may, of course, mean little" (p. xxvi). They add that it "makes good sense" to them (p. xxvi).
16e886deb60d: The familiar pairing of an allergy of the body with an obsession of the mind isn't in the Doctor's Opinion. In the Big Book it's in two members' stories (pp. 261, 355). Bill W. credits it to Silkworth in <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957, after 1950).
471fec4032d1: The craving, in the doctor's words
bae017ddc1f0: Silkworth's longer statement (pp. xxvii–xxxii) comes back to the craving again and again: - <0>It's physical, and it's treated first.</0> An alcoholic ought first to be freed from his physical craving for liquor, which often takes a hospital procedure, before psychological measures can be of most benefit (pp. xxvii–xxviii). - <1>It's the mark of a type.</1> The craving belongs to chronic alcoholics and never occurs in the temperate drinker. "These allergic types can never safely use alcohol in any form at all" (p. xxviii). - <2>It takes over once drinking starts.</2> He describes men who worked for months on a deal, took a drink a day or two before it closed, and "the phenomenon of craving at once became paramount to all other interests" (p. xxix), so they missed the appointment. "These men were not drinking to escape; they were drinking to overcome a craving beyond their mental control." (p. xxx) - <3>It's what all types share.</3> He lists several kinds of alcoholic, then says they have "one symptom in common" (p. xxx): they can't start drinking without the craving developing. It "has never been, by any treatment with which we are familiar, permanently eradicated" (p. xxx).
4a884b9e910d: How sure the book is about the allergy
7790f8eb740e: The text is careful: - Silkworth: "We believe, and so suggested a few years ago" (p. xxviii) that it is a manifestation of an allergy; and later, the craving "may be" one (p. xxx). - The A.A. members: "The doctor's theory that we have an allergy to alcohol interests us." (p. xxvi) As laymen they can't judge its soundness, but as ex-problem drinkers "his explanation makes good sense" (p. xxvi).
cbd2a73c0053: What they're sure of is the physical side itself. They write that "the body of the alcoholic is quite as abnormal as his mind" (p. xxvi), and "any picture of the alcoholic which leaves out this physical factor is incomplete" (p. xxvi).
1a483ab8c23c: The allergy isn't the doctor's whole picture. Between drinks, he says, the alcoholic is "restless, irritable and discontented" (p. xxviii) until he can feel again the ease a few drinks bring. After the spree comes remorse and a firm resolution, repeated over and over (p. xxix). He doesn't think alcoholism is "entirely a problem of mental control" (p. xxix), but he also says there is very little hope "unless this person can experience an entire psychic change" (p. xxix).
57adaf3d3b8d: Chapter 2 says the same from the members' side. Once the alcoholic takes any alcohol, "something happens, both in the bodily and mental sense" (p. 22). But because the cycle can't start without the first drink, "the main problem of the alcoholic centers in his mind, rather than in his body" (p. 23).
0d9f27c57163: Where the allergy-and-obsession pairing comes from
f3db782c43c1: The two-part phrase, often quoted as if it were the Big Book's own definition, doesn't appear in the Doctor's Opinion or the 1939 chapters. In the Big Book it turns up in members' stories. In "He Sold Himself Short" (Part I), the writer recalls being told that drinking was "a fatal illness made up of an allergy plus an obsession" (p. 261). In "It Might Have Been Worse" (Part II), the writer says the explanation of alcoholism as "an allergy of the body and an obsession of the mind" (p. 355) cleared up a lot for him. The 1939 chapters do speak of obsession in their own words: the idea that he will somehow control and enjoy his drinking "is the great obsession of every abnormal drinker" (p. 30).
78d5b03280a5: Bill W., writing in 1957, credits the pairing to Silkworth: "the obsession of the mind that compels us to drink and the allergy of the body that condemns us to go mad or die" (<0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) reports that Bill later said Silkworth used "allergy" knowing it wasn't exact: "He knew this was a misnomer" (<2>Pass It On</2>, 1984). Both books are after 1950, and both give Bill's later recollection; they're useful for where the phrase came from, not as part of the 1939 text.
dd0ac528daa9: It complicates it. The phrases are quoted accurately and Silkworth means them. But the book offers the allergy as a theory, hedged by both the doctor and the members, while holding firmly that the alcoholic's body is abnormal. The craving it describes starts with drinking, and the book pairs it with a mind that is "without defense against the first drink" (p. 24) and with Silkworth's own view that recovery takes a psychic change. d5ef1e5b3af1: <0>The claim.</0> Rarely "have we seen a person fail who has thoroughly followed our path" (p. 58). The word is "rarely," not "never."
0b7284ba1f5a: <0>Who doesn't recover.</0> Those who "cannot or will not" give themselves completely to the program (p. 58). The paragraph names both: "will not" is a refusal, "cannot" is an inability.
e63b9c66e938: <0>The usual reason.</0> Most are "constitutionally incapable of being honest with themselves" (p. 58). The book goes on: "There are such unfortunates." (p. 58) "They are not at fault; they seem to have been born that way." (p. 58) They can't grasp and develop a way of living "which demands rigorous honesty" (p. 58). And: "Their chances are less than average." (p. 58)
c3ac9433cd08: <0>A second group.</0> "There are those, too, who suffer from grave emotional and mental disorders" (p. 58), and "many of them do recover if they have the capacity to be honest" (p. 58).
75901aac3ca0: So the paragraph names two conditions for recovery: giving oneself completely to "this simple program," and the capacity to be honest. Where people fall short of the second, it calls them unfortunate, not guilty.
d844bad8ad1e: The "path" isn't left vague. The paragraph itself calls it "this simple program" (p. 58), and the next page introduces the Twelve Steps as "suggested as a program of recovery" (p. 59). In between, the book says what it asks of the reader. If you want what the members have and are willing to go to any length for it, "then you are ready to take certain steps" (p. 58). "At some of these we balked." (p. 58) And it begs the reader "to be fearless and thorough from the very start" (p. 58).
a1851cde3c2e: Then, right after the Steps, the book heads off the idea that "thoroughly" means flawlessly. "No one among us has been able to maintain anything like perfect adherence to these principles." (p. 60) "We are not saints." (p. 60) "We claim spiritual progress rather than spiritual perfection." (p. 60)

e94887fb8dbd: "Recovered" or "recovering": which word does the Big Book use?
b24eaafd8420: The Big Book's members call themselves "recovered." The 1939 Foreword opens with "more than one hundred men and women who have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii), and Chapter 2 says of the thousands they know, "Nearly all have recovered." (p. 17).
d5319ac825fa: The phrase "recovering alcoholic" is not in the fourth-edition Big Book. In our sources it appears in later books: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980), <1>Pass It On</1> (1984), P-16 (2018) and the current Service Manual.
a70cebafef5a: But "recovered" in the book doesn't mean cured or able to drink again. The same text says "We are not cured of alcoholism" and calls what members have "a daily reprieve contingent on the maintenance of our spiritual condition" (p. 85).
39fee1ec1402: The book also uses "recovering" for someone in the process: the husband "who is recovering" (p. 122). The word isn't foreign to it; the self-description is "recovered."
8781e9901f71: The word runs through the book: - The Foreword to the First Edition: the members "have recovered from a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii), and "To show other alcoholics precisely how we have recovered is the main purpose of this book." (p. xiii). - Dr. Silkworth's letter: "This man and over one hundred others appear to have recovered." (p. xxv). - Chapter 2: "Nearly all have recovered." (p. 17). "They have solved the drink problem." (p. 17). Readers are told the book will explain how "we have recovered from a hopeless condition of mind and body" (p. 20), followed by "clear-cut directions … showing how we recovered" (p. 29). - Chapter 7: the prospect's attention is drawn to the member "as a person who has recovered" (p. 90). - Chapter 9: "We have recovered, and have been given the power to help others." (p. 132). "We, who have recovered from serious drinking, are miracles of mental health." (p. 133). - Chapter 10: "An alcoholic who has recovered" can talk to another employee (p. 146).
a63d96f6a8fd: The fourth-edition title page reads "The Story of How Many Thousands of Men and Women Have Recovered from Alcoholism" (p. iii). Later A.A. writing keeps the word: in 1955 the Foreword to the Second Edition counted membership as "far above 150,000 recovered alcoholics" (p. xv), and <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957) says that clergymen and physicians are the experts and "we, the recovered alcoholics, are their assistants" (<1>A.A. Comes of Age</1>, 1957).
c16314dd92b3: What "recovered" does and doesn't mean in the book
5421daafacd6: The book is careful about what has been recovered from: - Not from alcoholism as a condition. "We know that no real alcoholic ever recovers control." (p. 30). "Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic." (p. 33). - Not once and for all. "We are not cured of alcoholism." (p. 85). The reprieve is daily and depends on the member's spiritual condition (p. 85). Step Ten's work "should continue for our lifetime" (p. 84). - What members say they have recovered from is "a seemingly hopeless state of mind and body" (p. xiii): the drink problem is solved (p. 17), so long as they keep in fit spiritual condition (p. 85).
904ab59fb5d0: The verb appears for someone in the middle of the process: - Chapter 9 opens by saying the members' "women folk have suggested certain attitudes a wife may take with the husband who is recovering" (p. 122). The chapter adds that "dad, though marvelously improved, is still convalescing" (p. 127). - Chapter 10: an employee who drinks "and is still trying to recover" will be honest about it (p. 146). - A later-edition footnote to Chapter 8 speaks of a woman alcoholic "whether she is still drinking or is recovering in A.A." (p. 104).
010a9a8a8881: What doesn't appear anywhere in the fourth-edition text, stories included, is the label "recovering alcoholic." "Recovered alcoholic(s)" appears in a few personal stories (pp. 273–274, 442).
27666e2ff955: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> (1980): Dr. Bob's adult years "as an active and then as a recovering alcoholic" (<1>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</1>, 1980).
40c7b7885230: <0>Pass It On</0> (1984) uses "recovering alcoholics" in its narrative of the 1930s and early 1940s .
293aa292b198: <0>The A.A. Group</0> (P-16, 2018): members may tell nonalcoholics "that we are recovering alcoholics" (P-16, 2018); GSO staff members "are themselves recovering alcoholics" (P-16, 2018).

7163a91aab5f: The 1939 text describes its members as recovered: rescued from a hopeless state, with the drink problem solved on a spiritual basis as a daily reprieve, and never able to drink safely again. "Recovering" as an identity is later usage. Neither the Big Book nor the later books in our sources say one word is right and the other wrong; this page only reports which word each source uses.

314581274bf3: Does the Big Book say "relapse is part of recovery"? What does it say about a slip?
101aca6b6669: No. "Relapse is part of recovery" is not in the Big Book or anywhere else in our sources.
8c5978586f8d: The program text's fullest word on it is to a wife whose husband comes home drunk: "Though it is infinitely better that he have no relapse at all, as has been true with many of our men, it is by no means a bad thing in some cases." (p. 120). In those cases he sees that he must "redouble his spiritual activities if he expects to survive" (p. 120).
67e8d30922b2: So the text neither treats relapse as an expected stage nor writes off the person who drinks again. It treats drinking as deadly ("to drink is to die," p. 66), and it treats the man who slips and keeps trying with patience (pp. 120, 147).
f0206529e737: All our sources were searched for "part of recovery," "relapse," "slip" and their forms, with page breaks joined. "Part of recovery" turns up once, in a story where "Commitment and service were part of recovery" (p. 345). Nothing in any book says relapse is part of recovery.
8061ea455cb2: In the program text, "relapse" appears at pp. 26, 31, 35, 120 and 125. "Slip" meaning a drink appears at p. 100 ("We have seen others slip when the family came back too soon") and p. 139 (an executive who "did slip and was fired"). At p. 84 ("Self-seeking will slip away") and p. 110 (friends who "slipped away") it means something else.
7470d86a8cc6: <0>The danger.</0> Of the remedies they tried before A.A., the book says that in some instances there was "brief recovery, followed always by a still worse relapse" (p. 31). "Commencing to drink after a period of sobriety, we are in a short time as bad as ever." (p. 33). Chapter 3 is written to describe "the mental states that precede a relapse into drinking, for obviously this is the crux of the problem" (p. 35). Bill: if an alcoholic didn't work with others "he would surely drink again, and if he drank, he would surely die" (p. 15). "And with us, to drink is to die." (p. 66).
a9ada318c624: <0>Its causes.</0> Newcomers who kept certain facts to themselves: "Almost invariably they got drunk." (p. 73). Resentment brings it back (p. 66). Family quarrels and old affairs dug up again: "In most cases, the alcoholic survived this ordeal without relapse, but not always." (p. 125).
c9386b5acd74: <0>When it happens.</0> The passage that speaks most fully to a relapse in a man who has started the program is in "To Wives" (p. 120). Read in full, it says: - If you are satisfied he really wants to get over drinking, "you need not be alarmed" (p. 120). - "Though it is infinitely better that he have no relapse at all, as has been true with many of our men, it is by no means a bad thing in some cases." (p. 120). - He will see at once that he must "redouble his spiritual activities if he expects to survive" (p. 120). Don't remind him of his spiritual deficiency; "Cheer him up and ask him how you can be still more helpful." (p. 120). - "If he gets drunk, don't blame yourself." (p. 120). "God has either removed your husband's liquor problem or He has not. If not, it had better be found out right away." (p. 120).
8385a3127ece: <0>Falling short in daily life.</0> In Chapter 7: "Of course, we all fall much below this standard many times. But we must try to repair the damage immediately lest we pay the penalty by a spree." (p. 99).
996749edea9a: <0>At work.</0> "In case he does stumble, even once, you will have to decide whether to let him go." (p. 147). If you are sure he doesn't mean business, discharge him; if you are sure he is doing his utmost, "you may wish to give him another chance" (p. 147). A man still trying to recover who does get drunk "will tell you about it even if it means the loss of his job" (p. 146).
10e81c2700ea: So "by no means a bad thing in some cases" is as far as the program text goes. It says that, and it says no relapse is "infinitely better." It never says relapse is needed, normal, or a stage everyone goes through.
14a110fde2aa: The Foreword to the Second Edition: of alcoholics who came to A.A. and really tried, "50% got sober at once and remained that way; 25% sobered up after some relapses" (p. xx), and among the rest, those who stayed showed improvement (p. xx). That is 1955, after Dr. Bob's death.
4a41613e913a: The early stories and Bill's essays
c0ca0463d034: Slips were written about openly from the start: - Two stories printed in the 1939 first edition, "The Back-Slider" and "The Seven Month Slip" (since dropped, now in <0>Experience, Strength and Hope</0>, 2003), are about men who drank again after one or two years sober. Both put it down to drifting from the program and relying on themselves, and both came back to friends who welcomed them. One says the fellowship "treated me as though nothing had happened" (Experience, Strength and Hope, 2003). - Dr. Bob's own story (1939) says he carries the message partly because each time "I take out a little more insurance for myself against a possible slip" (p. 181). - "He Sold Himself Short" (Part I, set in 1937–38) tells of a deliberate drunk a few months after the writer's start: "That was my only slip. It taught me a valuable lesson." (p. 265), namely that inventory has to be taken every day (pp. 264–265). - Bill W.'s 1946 Grapevine essay on membership says most early members "would have been thrown out because they slipped too much" (P-17) if the groups' early rules had been enforced, and of those who slip: "Some of these have become our most respected and best loved." (P-17).
6ceac62cc846: Later books, all after 1950: - <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0> (1957): at first slips were "always a genuine catastrophe" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957); by 1955, "Slips are a very serious difficulty, but as a group we take them in stride." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). - <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) quotes an undated letter of Bill's about members two or three years sober who slipped: he knew of none who hadn't, in a sense, benefited, and "The slip invariably kicks them upstairs instead of down." (Pass It On, 1984). The same letter calls these slips a lot of worry for the families (Pass It On, 1984). That is the nearest thing in our sources to the saying, and it is about what a slip can teach, not a claim that relapse is a necessary part of recovery. - <2>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</2> (1980) says that of the Akron members counted in February 1937, half "had or would have some sort of slip" (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980), and "For most, however, the slip was the convincer." It says drinking again is deadly, that no relapse is infinitely better, and that in some cases a relapse is "by no means a bad thing" (p. 120), the next sentence saying the man sees he must redouble his spiritual activities. Its tone toward the person who slips and is still trying is patient: a wife told not to lecture him, a possible second chance from the employer, and, in the early stories, a welcome back. 78811d7d7c12: No. You don't have to belong to a religion or accept anyone else's idea of God. The Big Book says "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and about…
cfc4af6fd634: Do I have to be religious to work the Steps?
2e3947cc5f62: No. You don't have to belong to a religion or accept anyone else's idea of God. The Big Book says "we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47), and about half the first members thought they were atheists or agnostics (p. 44).
22cbcf4c1a4b: What the book does ask for is a willingness to believe in a Power greater than yourself. It calls this the starting point, and says that is enough to begin (p. 47).
b70fb8452918: The book is open that it is a spiritual book and that it talks about God (p. 45). Five of the Twelve Steps name God or Him. It doesn't pretend otherwise; it leaves the meaning of the word to you.
5581d611000d: What the book asks for at the start
51f4ae3f7047: Chapter 4 (pp. 44–57), "We Agnostics," was written for the reader this question is about. Its main points, in order: - Something like half the original fellowship "thought we were atheists or agnostics" (p. 44). - The book is "spiritual as well as moral," and so "we are going to talk about God" (p. 45). Here the writers expect the agnostic's face to fall, and say they've shared his doubt; some of them had been "violently anti-religious" (p. 45). - They found they "did not need to consider another's conception of God" (p. 46). Their own conception, however inadequate, was enough to begin. - "When, therefore, we speak to you of God, we mean your own conception of God" (p. 47). - The one question needed at the start: "Do I now believe, or am I even willing to believe, that there is a Power greater than myself?" (p. 47) Someone who can say yes to that is "on his way" (p. 47). - How each member conceives of that Power varies widely in the stories, and these "are questions for each individual to settle for himself" (p. 50).
06476020d9a6: Where the book is not neutral
a391a7bc4030: To be fair to the text, Chapter 4 isn't indifferent about God. It argues, at length, that faith is more reasonable than unbelief (pp. 48–55). It puts the choice starkly: "either God is everything or else He is nothing" (p. 53). It asks agnostics to "lay aside prejudice, even against organized religion" (p. 49), and it ends with the story of a man who thought he was an atheist and came to "conscious companionship with his Creator" (p. 56).
24a5e3764b3d: So the book hopes the reader will come to a faith of his own. What it doesn't do is require any religion, church, creed or particular conception of God to start, or to work the Steps.
47f37e4b965f: Appendix II, written after the first printing (p. 567), says the "spiritual experience" or "spiritual awakening" the book talks about is a personality change, and that most of these develop slowly (p. 567). Interestingly, it uses "religious experiences" as another name for the same personality changes (p. 567). It then says any alcoholic can recover "provided he does not close his mind to all spiritual concepts" (p. 568), and that "no one need have difficulty with the spirituality of the program" (p. 568). Willingness, honesty and open-mindedness are what's essential (p. 568).
ed9c08998ed6: How a member is told to talk about it
db538b73853d: Chapter 7 tells the person carrying the message how to handle this with a newcomer: - With an agnostic or atheist, make it plain he doesn't have to agree with your conception of God. 0ec064f36fea: What is the Right of Appeal, and why does the minority matter?
ccbccaca4ba2: The Right of Appeal is Bill W.'s Fifth Concept (1962): throughout A.A.'s world service structure, "minority opinion will be heard and personal grievances receive careful consideration" (p. 574).
b5459f0fb19e: It has two parts. A minority that thinks the majority is badly wrong is encouraged to file a minority report, and on a grave issue has a duty to take it to the General Service Conference. And anyone working in the structure, paid or unpaid, may petition the General Service Board over a personal grievance "without prejudice or fear of reprisal" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
9921af8a4655: Why: minorities are often right, and even when they're wrong they force a real debate. "The well-heard minority, therefore, is our chief protection against an uninformed, misinformed, hasty or angry majority" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
3a451ac99a5e: A related idea is older than the Concepts. In 1946, writing about who should pay for clubs, Bill said that "the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority" (P-17, Money, 1946).
89a9dc477c76: The Long Form of the Traditions protects the individual first: A.A. "may refuse none who wish to recover," and membership should never depend "upon money or conformity" (p. 563).
c0ecb6382310: Bill's 1946 essay on money applies it to a disagreement. Most members liked clubs, but not all, so club support should come from those who wanted them: "But the majority ought not to try to coerce the minority into supporting clubs they do not want or need" (P-17, Money, 1946).
bdb928cf0aa3: His 1947 essay on government lists among A.A.'s freedoms "no one set in personal authority over anyone else" (P-17, Will A.A. Ever Have a Personal Government?, 1947).
2065005e0c34: The 1955 Conference Charter built minority protection into elections: delegates are chosen "by a two-thirds written ballot or by lot" (The A.A. Service Manual, 2024–2026, Appendix K, Original Conference Charter, 1955).
6b4bbef97bf1: <0>Appeal.</0> All minorities, "whether in our staffs, committees, corporate boards or among the Trustees," should be encouraged to file minority reports when they think the majority is in considerable error (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Where a wrong decision could seriously affect A.A. as a whole, the minority should treat presenting a report to the Conference as an actual duty.
de423c61d9b1: <0>Why minorities matter.</0> "In granting this traditional ‘Right of Appeal,’ we recognize that minorities frequently can be right" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). Even when partly or wholly wrong, they compel a thorough debate.
8ff760f94a6a: <0>Petition.</0> Any person in the structure may carry a personal grievance directly to the General Service Board. Bill expected it to be used seldom, but "its very existence will always tend to restrain those in authority from unjust uses of their power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
7fab1d4d3617: <0>Where it comes from.</0> Bill ties it to A.A.'s membership freedoms: "any alcoholic is a member of A.A. the moment he says so; we cannot take away his right to belong" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). "Neither can we force our members to believe anything or pay anything" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).
e80a12d65c23: <0>How it already worked in 1962.</0> - <1>Electing delegates.</1> Unless a candidate gets two-thirds of the assembly, his name goes in a hat with the minority's choices, and the delegate is drawn by lot. Bill admits this sometimes sets aside the simple-majority rule, and says it has strengthened the spirit of democracy: no discontented minority trails behind the winner. - <2>The Conference's own habit.</2> "Unless it has been absolutely unavoidable, the Conference has usually refused to take important decisions on anything less than a two-thirds vote" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V). - <3>The trustees' check.</3> Under the Charter, a Conference vote binds the trustees only at two-thirds of a quorum, so a narrow majority can't force them; they can insist on more debate.
b64a7e7426a7: Bill closes with Alexis de Tocqueville's warning against the "tyranny" of apathetic, self-seeking, uninformed or angry majorities, and adds the opposite danger: "the even worse tyranny of very small minorities invested with absolute power" (Twelve Concepts for World Service, Concept V).

1d33fed44f59: Read in place, each "selfish" is something to get rid of, and each "unselfish" something to aim for (with one neutral exception, noted): - Bill, in hospital: a doctor told him that though he was "certainly selfish and foolish," he had been seriously ill (p. 7). - The real alcoholic is sensible about everything except liquor, "but in that respect he is incredibly dishonest and selfish" (p. 21). - The actor who wants to run the show may be "mean, egotistical, selfish and dishonest" (p. 61). Even when he's kind, he's "really a self-seeker" (p. 61). - "Selfishness—self-centeredness! That, we think, is the root of our troubles" (p. 62). (p. 62). - In the resentment inventory: "Where had we been selfish, dishonest, self-seeking and frightened?" (p. 67). On sex conduct, each relationship is tested: "was it selfish or not?" (p. 69). - At home: "Selfish and inconsiderate habits have kept the home in turmoil" (p. 82). - Chapter 8, written in the voice of alcoholics' wives, says they "were not above selfishness or dishonesty" (p. 116). (p. 86). 3c0c6241e10a: The Serenity Prayer is not in the Big Book's program text (pp. 1–164), its forewords or its appendices. It appears only in some of the members' stories at the back of the fourth edition.
c99249a3ed22: It came into A.A. in New York in the early 1940s. A member saw it in a newspaper obituary notice and brought it to the office, and A.A. began printing it on cards and putting one in every letter it sent out.
0d7dbd7157ba: Bill W. wrote in 1957: "No one can tell for sure who first wrote the Serenity Prayer" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). He listed several claims, including the one that it was by Reinhold Niebuhr.
70be0dd716c4: The sources disagree on the date (1941 or early 1942), on the exact wording of the clipping, and on the name of the man who paid for the first cards.
c0988b0df15b: A search of the whole fourth edition finds the prayer only in the personal stories, for example pp. 345, 357, 401, 419 and 559. The word "serenity" does appear in the main text, in other senses: Bill's peace and serenity after his experience at Towns Hospital (p. 14), the hope "to match calamity with serenity" (p. 68), and the promise "We will comprehend the word serenity and we will know peace" (p. 84). None of these is the prayer.
d8a22f0f06b4: How it came into A.A.: Bill's account (1957)
77cd4a4bd856: In <0>A.A. Comes of Age</0>, Bill says that just before Ruth Hock, the office secretary, left in early 1942, "newsman Jack," a New York member, showed them a clipping (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). It was an obituary notice, and under it were the words: "God grant us the serenity to accept the things we cannot change, courage to change the things we can, and wisdom to know the difference." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
986a2aa96779: "Never had we seen so much A.A. in so few words." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). A friend, Howard, came into the office and offered to pay for printing it on cards to go into every piece of mail (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). They did that for several years, and the prayer quickly came into general use, alongside "our two other favorites, the Lord's Prayer and the Prayer of St. Francis" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
272cabe6796d: On who wrote it, Bill says some credited the early Greeks, some an anonymous English poet, some an American naval officer, and that Jack Alexander, who had looked into it, "attributes it to the Rev. Reinhold Niebuhr of the Union Theological Seminary" (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). Bill's conclusion: "Anyhow, we have the prayer and it is said thousands of times daily." (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957).
452226aba42d: The later biography gives more detail. It says the prayer was found in the "In Memoriam" column of an early June 1941 edition of the New York Herald-Tribune (Pass It On, 1984). It gives the notice's wording, addressed to "Mother" and beginning "Mother — God grant me the serenity to accept the things I cannot change" (Pass It On, 1984), going on with "I can" in the second line and ending "Goodbye."
733c2ee52855: It quotes Ruth Hock: "Jack C. appeared at the office one morning, and he showed me the obituary notice" (Pass It On, 1984), and she copied it to use in letters to groups and loners. In her account, "Horace C. had the idea of printing it on cards and paid for the first printing" (Pass It On, 1984). Elsewhere <0>Pass It On</0> notes that in his 1957 book Bill called Horace C. "Howard A." (Pass It On, 1984), so the two accounts may name the same man.
544b95e6341b: A note in <0>Pass It On</0> says the prayer's origins are obscure: it may go back to the philosopher Boethius, about 500 A.D.; it is usually credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, a 20th-century theologian, who in turn credited an 18th-century theologian (Pass It On, 1984). Our copy of that note is damaged by the scan, so the second theologian's name can't be read with confidence.
c6ef7348b0fe: <0>Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers</0> quotes an early Ohio member, Oscar W., describing the friction between the Midwest and New York in the 1940s: "I don't like the Serenity Prayer. New York brought it in, and we resented it." (Dr. Bob and the Good Oldtimers, 1980). To him it felt like the Oxford Group's praying coming back.
1d610b0679ea: Later A.A. literature describes the prayer as a common part of meetings. P-16, <0>The A.A. Group</0> (© 2018), describing how a chairperson usually opens a meeting with the Preamble, adds: "Some call for a moment of silence and/or recite the Serenity Prayer" (P-16). 2430c68e69ba: <0>When.</0> Bill (1957) puts it just before Ruth Hock left in early 1942 (A.A. Comes of Age, 1957). <1>Pass It On</1> (1984) says an early June 1941 newspaper (Pass It On, 1984).
